subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: How far? The extent of chemical change
themeLabel: How much, how fast and how far?
bigPicture: Many reactions don't go to completion: they reach a dynamic equilibrium where forward and backward reactions run at the same rate. The equilibrium constant K measures how far the reaction gets, and Le Châtelier's principle predicts how the mixture responds when conditions change.

keyIdeas.cue: What are the features of dynamic equilibrium?
keyIdeas.answer: Closed system; forward and reverse rates equal; concentrations (and macroscopic properties such as colour and pressure) constant, but not necessarily equal; both reactions continue. Applies to physical systems (e.g. liquid–vapour in a sealed flask) and chemical ones.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you write an equilibrium constant expression?
keyIdeas.answer: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD (homogeneous): K = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ), using equilibrium concentrations.

keyIdeas.cue: What does the size of K tell you?
keyIdeas.answer: K ≫ 1: almost complete, products dominate. K > 1: products favoured. K = 1: similar amounts. K < 1: reactants favoured. K ≪ 1: hardly any reaction. K changes only with temperature. For the reverse reaction K' = 1/K; doubling the coefficients squares K.

keyIdeas.cue: How does Le Châtelier's principle predict changes?
keyIdeas.answer: A system at equilibrium responds to partially oppose a change. Adding a reactant → shifts right. Higher pressure → shifts to fewer gas moles. Higher temperature → shifts in the endothermic direction, and K changes (falls for an exothermic forward reaction). A catalyst changes neither the position nor K; equilibrium is just reached faster. Also applies to heterogeneous equilibria such as a gas dissolving, X(g) ⇌ X(aq).

keyIdeas.cue: What is the reaction quotient Q (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Same expression as K but with concentrations at any moment. Q < K: net forward reaction. Q > K: net reverse. Q = K: at equilibrium.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you calculate K or equilibrium concentrations (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Use an ICE table (Initial, Change, Equilibrium) in mol dm⁻³, with changes in the mole ratio. If K is very small, assume [reactant]eq ≈ [reactant]initial to avoid quadratics (which are not required). Only homogeneous equilibria are assessed.

keyIdeas.cue: How is K linked to ΔG⦵ (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K. Large K ↔ large negative ΔG⦵. See also R1.4 for ΔG = ΔG⦵ + RT ln Q.

keyTerms.def: Forward and reverse rates equal; concentrations constant; closed system.
Ratio of product to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, each to the power of its coefficient.
An equilibrium shifts to partially counteract an imposed change.
All species in the same phase.

workedExamples.title: Le Châtelier
workedExamples.prompt: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Predict the effect on yield of NH₃ of (a) raising pressure, (b) raising temperature.
steps: (a) 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas: higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles → yield rises.
(b) Forward is exothermic: higher T favours the endothermic reverse reaction → yield falls and K decreases.
workedExamples.answer: (a) increases; (b) decreases. Industry uses a compromise temperature for an acceptable rate.

workedExamples.title: ICE table (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: 1.00 mol H₂ and 1.00 mol I₂ in a 1.00 dm³ flask reach equilibrium with 1.56 mol HI. Calculate K for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI.
steps: Change: HI +1.56, so H₂ and I₂ each −0.78.

misconceptions.wrong: At equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
Adding a catalyst increases the equilibrium yield.
misconceptions.right: It speeds up both directions equally; yield and K are unchanged.

misconceptions.wrong: Increasing concentration of a reactant changes K.
misconceptions.right: Only temperature changes K; the position shifts so that the ratio returns to K.

practice.prompt: Deduce the equilibrium constant expression for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g).
Predict and explain the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of the equilibrium above.
checkpoints: Forward and reverse rates increase equally

practice.prompt: For a reaction with K = 4.0, a mixture has Q = 10. Determine the direction of net reaction.
checkpoints: Net reverse reaction (towards reactants) until Q = K

practice.prompt: Calculate ΔG⦵ at 298 K for a reaction with K = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵.

paper1A.stem: What is the expression for K for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)?
For an exothermic forward reaction, what happens to K when temperature rises?
K for A ⇌ B is 4. What is K for B ⇌ A?
Which change shifts N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) to the right?
paper1A.why: Fewer moles on the left; lower pressure favours more moles.

paper1B.data: Equilibrium data at 700 K for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: [H₂] = 0.010, [I₂] = 0.010, [HI] = 0.070 mol dm⁻³. A second mixture has [H₂] = 0.020, [I₂] = 0.020, [HI] = 0.10.
paper1B.prompt: Calculate K and Q for the second mixture, and state the direction of change.
paper1B.answer: K = 0.070²/(0.010 × 0.010) = 49. Q = 0.10²/(0.020 × 0.020) = 25. Q < K, so net forward reaction (more HI forms).

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.

errorHints.hint: Only temperature changes K; catalysts change neither K nor position.
Count gas moles on each side before predicting pressure effects; ignore solids and liquids.
In ICE tables, use concentrations (divide moles by volume) and apply the mole ratio to the change row.
Predict + justify: give the direction AND the Le Châtelier reason, and say what happens to K.

linkingQuestions.prompt: How do ΔG⦵ and K describe the same equilibrium (AHL)?
How is Ka an equilibrium constant for acid ionisation?

links.gap: No items on K calculations with ICE tables (R2.3.6) or on ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K (R2.3.7); Q is covered (k17, fc-chem-r2-14).
